utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. There are two matters I'd like to deal with before we continue to hear the evidence. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will now then issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution motion for testimony of Momcilo Krajisnik to be presented viva voce, filed on the 23rd of July, 2013, wherein the Prosecution requests that the testimony of Momcilo Krajisnik be presented viva voce on the basis of his position during the period relevant to the indictment, the nature of the expected testimony, the expected volume of material to be submitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter, as well as the fact that as Krajisnik has already been found to be a witness of low credibility, the Chamber can be in a better position to assess his credibility with a viva voce testimony. The accused filed a response on the 24th of July, 2013, noting that although in principle he favours viva voce witness presentation, he opposes the request unless the Chamber is willing to give him additional time to conclude the presentation of his case. Having considered Krajisnik's position during the conflict, his close proximity to the accused, and the nature of his prospective testimony, including the fact that he's expected to refute the allegation in the indictment pertaining to joint criminal enterprise which go to the core of the accused's alleged responsibility, the Chamber considers that it is in the interests of justice that Momcilo Krajisnik be heard viva voce. The Prosecution's motion is therefore granted. We'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before or while we're doing that. First of all, thank you for ruling on that motion quickly. Secondly, on Monday we're going to hear the testimony of Mendeljev Djuric and on Tuesday Franc Kos. Both of those people are being transferred to the Tribunal and are being assigned counsel by the Registry to assist them pursuant to the Rules, and we would ask that the Chamber allow counsel for each of them to be present during their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no position from the Prosecution? It is so granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's one further scheduling issue then. We are supposed to resume after the recess on the 27th, Tuesday, August, but due to some internal matters we are going to resume the next day, i.e., Wednesday, the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. When we left off yesterday we were talking about Sanski Most and we were talking about evidence that in Mr. Brown's report goes toward your conclusion which you stated in page 26, I'll just remind everybody, in your critique of Mr. Brown, that the conclusion of this paragraph, which was Ewan Brown's paragraph 2.35, undoubtedly suggests that the target of military operations in Sanski Most were residential areas, i.e., civilians and not Muslim and Croat armed formations. And you said basically something similar yesterday at 41952 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not been receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you -- do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear the gentleman but no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do you hear me now in the language you understand? No. How about now? Do you hear me in Serbian? If we could check the connection of the headphone. Do you hear me, sir, now? Let's check whether it works now? No. General, I hope you can hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning again, General. I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When we left off yesterday, we were starting to talk about operations in Sanski Most, and I'd begun in connection with page 26 in English of your report, where you critique -- criticise Mr. Brown for finding that the target of military operations in Sanski Most were residential areas, i.e., civilians and not Muslim and Croat armed formations. And you said something similar yesterday at 41952, where you said: "I didn't find a single order, a single document where the 6th Sana Brigade would be asked to disarm only Muslims and Croats, rather, that brigade is ordered to collect the weapons illegally owned by the population, irrespective of their ethnicity." And later on at the bottom of the page you said: "That brigade was tasked with preventing inter-ethnic conflicts and with disarming those who had illegal weapons." So that's what we're -- topic we're continuing on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P03313, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I don't have the transcript of the trial on the desktop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, while this is coming up, again P03313, this is a document I'm sure you've seen, it's cited in Mr. Brown's report at footnotes 322 and 389. It's the combat task of disarmament written by TO Commander Anicic and you're familiar with this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this document starts off saying that in some parts of the municipality with a Muslim and Croat population the Green Berets were inserted, et cetera. And it talks about in paragraph 2: "In co-ordination with the units of the 6th Brigade, complete control of the territory in order to ensure stable functioning of the government and to create conditions for unobstructed life and work." And then number 3: "The 6th Brigade, in co-ordinated action with the TO, is undertaking combat operations in the Sanski Most municipality area in order to disarm enemy forces ..." And if we go to the next page in the English, this document isn't dated, but it states: "Stand by for attack at 5 a.m. on 26 May ..." And then you see in paragraph 5 and 6 at the very beginning that it orders defence of Serbian neighbourhoods. So you would say that this document supports you, your thesis, correct, because it talks about disarming the enemy formations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a technical correction here. It was not the Serbian Territorial Defence. It was the staff of the Territorial Defence without any affiliation, either Serbian or anybody else's. However, since it were -- acted in a co-ordinated action with the 6th Brigade, we can say that it was probably a unit of the TO staff and that most of its members were Serb fighters. This is an order issued by the commander of the staff of Territorial Defence which originated from the situation in Sanski Most, and the fact that in that area there were significant Muslim and Croatian forces that were very active. Since that area was far beyond the front lines that had been established in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serb forces did not have a choice. Since they launched operations they had to face them and engage them and neutralise those forces deep in their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So the shorter answer would have been yes, that it supports your thesis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can say that, yes, it supports the thesis that it was part of the process to disarm Muslim and Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and according to you, it would also be to disarm Serbs who illegally own weapons; correct? Because you said that's -- yesterday you said that that was the task, to disarm everybody, regardless of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you consider this a legitimate military order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I believe that this is a legitimate military order. Irrespective of how it looks, the factual situation in that area at that time was that there was a territory, there was a population, there were authorities, and the authorities had to have control over that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on now and look at some entries in diaries of members of the Crisis Staff that preceded this order, where they talk about the disarmament operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 23069, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, sir, what's coming up is the diary of a member of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff named Dr. Nenad Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have page 11 in the English and Serbian quickly just to establish a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So there we can see we're on 21st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go ahead two pages, please, to page 13 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There we've got "meeting." This Crisis Staff member's notes. "1. Disarm the population." 2 -- second point: "Not necessary to seize weapons if they own a valid permit. "Perform inspection ... "Seize all weapons by hook or by crook ..." A little further down: "Everyone resisting Serbian authorities will be expelled together with their families." Number 2 -- after that, sorry: "All extremists will be expelled from the municipality, while the authorities guarantee safety to all loyal citizens. "Disarming on Sunday." So this member of the ARK Crisis Staff is expressly referring to expelling families; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's referring to expelling extremists, and he adds to that "their families." Extremists, those who are not loyal, who have weapons without permission, and who do not comply with the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Now, very briefly, do you agree with me that the SOS in Sanski Most, the Serbian defence forces, that that was a paramilitary organisation of criminals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept such qualification. In order to assert something like that, one would have to have a list of those individuals, i.e., of those units and personal data for each and every member. We would have to know what they did in order to be able to say that they were organisations of criminals. In general terms, the Serbian defence forces appeared during a very brief period of time in the territory of Bosnian Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I've -- I don't want to cut you off, but I do have limited time and I think you've answered the question. And maybe if we have time, I'll show you a list of the SOS members later. Do you have any doubt that in this meeting the Crisis Staff member Davidovic is referring to expelling the families, Muslim and Croat families, who are considered extremists, not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he said that or perhaps it is just a note of something that somebody else said at that meeting. I'm not sure that he himself said that. He was in charge of the minutes of the meeting, so it may have been said by somebody else. It is about the resettling of extremists and their families. He uses the word "moving extremists and their families." I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And my question was: Do you have any doubt that what is being referred to in this meeting is the families of Muslims and Croats who are considered extremists, not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not specified. We can't find this in the document. The only thing that I can read here is those who resist Serbian authorities. We can assume that those were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go on to page 15 of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, may I tender that page? It's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. We don't believe that the witness has been able to confirm the accuracy of this. We also dispute the provenance and reliability of it. So when someone's private diary is being offered, we think that they ought to be here to testify before you for the truth or for the substance of the information contained in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, other pages of this diary have been admitted, so the provenance of the overall document has already been established for the sake of admission. The witness is testifying about what is going on in Sanski Most. He was not at this meeting but he has been able to comment on it through his knowledge, through his report of what happened in that Sanski Most and is able to say from reading this that he assumes that it is about people who resisted the authorities, meaning Muslims and Croats. So I think it's completely fair and I intend to show another page of this document and ask the witness about it. It fits with his report and testimony that only -- or he says that only armed formations were targeted. And the witness has also explained that Davidovic, he understands, was the note-taker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Part of this was admitted through 490, Witness KDZ490.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. The other -- if I go to the next document as well, the next page, perhaps we wait, I will show you how it is corroborated by other documents which are in evidence that are beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the fact that part of this diary has already been admitted, the Chamber has no difficulty with adding this page to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could go on now to page 15 in both languages. This page has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Here we see: "Crisis Staff Meeting." It's undated, but if we look at the conclusions, number 3 there is: "Protection of important buildings in Sanski Most - Colonel Basara and Anicic (waterworks, silo ...)" et cetera. And you may remember when we looked at the Crisis Staff decision of the 21st of May meeting, which was P02613, yesterday, that Crisis Staff decision appointed Basara in charge of protecting important buildings including the silo. So this should be, again looking at the earlier dates we looked at, Dr. Davidovic's notes of the 21st of May meeting of the Crisis Staff. And if you look down we see: "Colonel Basara - decree - calling them to hand in their weapons ..." So this refers to the disarmament operation which was referred to in the decision. Then we have the note: "Expelled from these areas forever." So this is the 21st of May meeting, it talks about protection of the silos, it talks about Basara and Anicic to put the plan of disarmament in place, ensuring peace in Sanski Most, that's what the 21st decision says, but this one, when they're meeting, what they don't write in their decision is there's a discussion about people being expelled from these areas forever; right? That's where a meeting where Basara, the 6th Krajina Brigade commander, is present.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key issue in my findings regarding those events, in reference to the notes that were kept by the said person, is probably the discussion at the meeting of the Crisis Staff. However, I never doubted any of the documents in my findings, either in terms of the authors or their contents. What I analysed, however, was the fact that the policy of the authorities and the army was not to expel the population from Sanski Most, because they explicitly ordered that protection should be offered to all the loyal population irrespective of their ethnicity. This is the main message regarding my attitude towards the situation in Sanski Most. There are people who may have said that extremists should be expelled, there's no doubt about that. There may have been inhumane or hostile attitude towards some people; however, what I analysed, what my expert analysis was about, was that that was not the official policy of the Serbian authorities and its army and police --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Bosnian Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. You keep repeating that and I understand that. But what you said and what you criticised Mr. Brown for was saying that Muslim and civilian population was targeted by the VRS, not just armed formations. And what I'm trying to show you is what is said behind the scenes, at the Crisis Staff before that order you consider legitimate came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 18, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Crisis Staff meeting, 25th of May, just before the disarmament combat starts. "Protection of important buildings ..." we saw that before, Davidovic has noted "done." "Organise two prisons ..." Persons to be arrested. "Do not arrest with weapons. "Civilians for exchange ..." So the day before the combat operation starts, this member of the Crisis Staff has listed: "Do not arrest with weapons. "Civilians for exchange ..." "Do no arrest with weapons," that means during the combat operation, if they come across somebody who's armed, don't take them prisoner, don't arrest them; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of any combat operation is the destruction of the enemy and that is quite legitimate. I cannot really tell what he meant here, but what I wish to say is that all those who are in the territory, under the control of the Serbian authorities, had the choice to hand-over their weapons and live peacefully. They opted for combat or fighting and that's when the actions occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. "Civilians for exchange." Very quickly, from what you know as a military expert, during the combat operations after 25th of May, in Sanski Most, were large numbers of civilians captured and held prisoner and then later exchanged? Muslim and Croat civilians I'm speaking of.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Procedures were conducted here of detaining a number of persons for whom it was subsequently established that they did not put up armed resistance to the army in that disarmament operation and they were subsequently, for the most part, released. And the policy was for the civilians to be released. When we talk about this item, civilians for exchange, at that time already there was strong pressure and the desire on the part of the Serbs to leave from areas under the control of Muslims and Croats to areas under Serb control. So there are other documents that attest to this. So what was left is for the civilians, Muslims and Croats, to be exchanged, for civilians, Serbs who were in territory under the control of Muslims and Croats. So in that sense, when you compare that and when you use this factual analysis, then you come to the point of why this is here, the civilians for exchange. But those who wanted to stay, who were loyal, there was no pressure at all exerted on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document about this same meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P03635. Now, if I could have English page 33, Serbian page 25. I read out the wrong number I think. P03329. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, this is the diary of the president of the Crisis Staff, Nedeljko Rasula. Did you know him at all in a personal capacity? If you could answer that quickly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to meet Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992/1993. I knew him during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps - I cannot be precise - but I think that perhaps it was sometime in the autumn of 1992 that I had the opportunity to meet him first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where? In Sanski Most or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not in Sanski Most. I think that it was during a meeting which was held in Bijeljina at that time, in the autumn. I cannot recall the details now. That was the first time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. These are his notes of the same meeting, 25th of May, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, if we can go back one page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you'll notice that they match Dr. Davidovic's, number 1, the same: "Information on security of important features." Number 3: "The disarmament plan and its beginning." Number 4: "... arrest of leaders ..." I want you to look at item 3: "Tuesday at 6.00 to 7.00 the operation begins. "The fighting will not stop until they surrender. "... no prisoners if armed. "Captured civilians to be used for exchanges." So he's written down a little bit more in detail than Dr. Davidovic did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, yes, next page. My copy's different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now: "No prisoners if armed." That means take no prisoners if armed; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he really meant by that I really cannot tell now, but I assume that that could have been that. However, we don't know who is saying this in order to be able to subject that to any kind of particular analysis because the Crisis Staff is not the one that can set combat rules for army units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Well, in that case let's please go to, very quickly, the meeting of 24 May --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go to same document, English page 31, Serbian page 25. Should be the 24th of May meeting. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I wasn't going to show this, but since you brought it up, the 24th of May, Crisis Staff meeting: "Colonel Basara proposed a strike at the strongest point." Next entry in item 3: "Colonel Anicic suggested Bojancic, Demisevci ..." and then some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in English. "Colonel Basara will prepare an operation against Demisevci evening. The proposal was not accepted. It was decided that it should be take place on Tuesday."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Although Colonel Basara is under the command of General Talic, these decisions on where to attack and when are being taken in consultation with the Crisis Staff members; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly for some reason, the Crisis Staff here suggested - and Colonel Basara probably accepted or gave up the -- or abandoned the previously planned action - we cannot really tell exactly how this process proceeded of co-ordinating. But I think in the continuation it says that it's possible that it's just being postponed from the evening to the morning or similar time, as it says here --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. My point --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My point is that these decisions are being taken in consultation with the Crisis Staff, the military decisions; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, military decisions -- or rather, the Crisis Staff does not make military decisions. The Crisis Staff monitors the situation, notes problems, and seeks to resolve them. If it's a matter of disarmament, that would be something that would be delegated to an army representative or a commander of a unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let -- let --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so in that sense they did co-ordinate --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just stop you because that's what I said was consultation, not that the Crisis Staff ordered. Let's go back to where we were on the 25th of May, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay: "Captured civilians to be used for exchange." That's unambiguously talking about taking -- capturing civilians and using them; correct? So Muslims civilians are going to be captured and used for exchanges; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no suggestion here of civilians being captured, but it would happen that, in an area, you could not make a selection of those who were being -- who were giving themselves up, especially if we're talking about the male population. So you could not immediately carry out a triage and then in such cases it would happen that civilians would be captured. This did happen, but if this did happen, then they would be used for an exchange. I don't see anyone here saying that civilians should be captured. For that reason, they wouldn't have to go into combat in order to capture civilians. They could assemble civilians from any settlement where they were loyal to the authorities and then exchange them. All of this applied to combat and understandably sometimes there would be an error and then a civilian would be brought in or captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. I don't want to belabour the point, but this doesn't say captured civilians to be released back to their homes. It doesn't say triage to be performed to make sure that captured civilians are not held unjustly. It says: "Captured civilians to be used ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This diary by Mr. Rasula is his notes, something that he drafted, where he noted things that he thought were of importance. This was not -- these are not notes from Crisis Staff meetings where we could see what was really said in the full sense of the word. I will just continue and where it says no capture with weapons and then it also says battles should continue until surrender. So these interpretations are conflicting. How can you say these two things and understand them? It's a question of how Rasula was taking his notes. So when there is combat, it's normal to assume that there were those captured, but at the bottom it says "no." So this would need to be analysed more carefully so that we would see the official document that was the result of the content of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that's my point exactly, sir, that the official document which we looked at, the Grmec order written by the TO commander, does not say "capture civilians for exchange," does not say "take no prisoners if armed." But that's what was discussed in meetings of the Crisis Staff in which Anicic and Basara were members. These are notes of a Crisis Staff meeting. So you can't just rely on the official version because it's unusual for an official document, an official order, to contain orders to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, that official orders usually do not contain paragraphs that would lead to crimes being committed, but in the same way we cannot accept that it was an official policy that somebody at some meeting made some comment or said something. Only what is stated in an official document in keeping with professional rules is something we could consider to be correct and official conduct. That there were official talks is -- that's something you could conclude on the basis of this, but that was not accepted and only documents would indicate what the actual position was of the authorities and of the army on certain issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll see that very soon. Let's go to the next page of the Serbian, staying where we are on the English, please, to the 26th of May Crisis Staff meeting. Did you know Major Veljko Brajic of the 1 KK?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I knew Major Veljko Brajic. I met him in 1994. He was the commander of the Doboj Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, that was later. Here he is in 26 of May, 1992, speaking at the Crisis Staff meeting. We see he talked about himself, his personality, gave a kind of background. He said, at least according to Rasula's notes, something along the lines of to establish a Serbian state in which the rule of law will apply. SDS decisions are not heeded here. Go down a bit. "In future work, we must make sure: "(a) that prisoners of war are to be taken over from the MUP, held overnight, and the most extreme among them isolated and punished so as not to walk on this earth ..." Now, that's not something you're ever going to see written in an order, is it, punish people so that they are not able to walk on the earth, but that's what Rasula wrote down that he said in this meeting. So you have to look beyond the official documents to see what the real intentions are, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this part, that they would not walk this earth, that's something that I would understand more in a symbolic light because anyone who's against the country and against those authorities, that's something that maybe he meant because that contradicts what he said at the top, to establish a Serbian state with rule of law. If you establish a state where the rule of law applies, you cannot then stop somebody from walking this earth. This is something that cannot be conceived and it's not something that can actually be implemented. So these are indicators that you could not really evaluate to say something like that, it's beyond any criteria. I really cannot tell what he wanted to say by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean by "can't be implemented," because after the disarmament operation there were Muslim individuals taken prisoner and beaten to death in Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were incidents where the outcome was death. There were individuals who took justice into their own hands and I'm not denying that, I never did. What I do deny is the existence of a plan for somebody to be beaten up, for prisoners of war to be mistreated, punished. The existence of such an intention, but there were such instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just quickly, could we go down to item (f) in the English. We need to go to the next page. Serbian page 26. And just very quickly here, we see that something else that Major Brajic said was that: "The announcements on Radio Sana are not censored. I just want to now go to P00725, look at one of these radio broadcasts. This is a radio broadcast of 27 May 1992 in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a transcript, I'm not going to play the tape, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to e-court 5, English; Serbian, page 4. Your Honours, while it's coming up I'll say that P00135 and P00122, it's the evidence provided by Faik Biscevic in this case, that he was one of the speakers on this tape on that date and authenticated it. Sorry, B/C/S -- Serbian page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So this was after -- the day after the meeting we just saw, the Crisis Staff meeting, the 26th of May, in which the 1 KK major said the extremists to be treated not to walk the earth. I want you to look at the female voice which should be at the top of your page. "We call upon the inhabitants of Pobrijezje to bring all their weapons and military equipment to the crossroads at the check-point by 1800 hours. If not, at exactly 1810 hours we will begin to shell the village. If the order is not complied with, we will not bear moral or material responsibility for the consequences of the shelling." And then we see "male voice, Faik Biscevic." And you're familiar with the Biscevic family, aren't you, of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of that family. We don't know each other, but I did hear that that was an old Muslim family in Sanski Most which was influential and had -- was a prominent family at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's look at what Faik Biscevic said on this tape. "That all Muslims and Croats unconditionally hand over all the weapons they possess legally and illegally and that they surrender to the Serbian army and government because this is a Serbian town. To avoid the soldiers having to use force to locate and seize weapons, it would be better to hand over the weapons voluntarily, otherwise Sana will continue to be destroyed until final capitulation. That is why we call upon the citizens of Sana, Muslims and Croats, to hand over their weapons straight away, which would be better for them to have their town continue to be destroyed ..." Now, when Faik Biscevic made that statement, he'd been brought there by soldiers of the 1 KK. He was forced to read that statement. He was a prisoner. He had guns pointed at him. I'm putting it to you that statement tells us exactly what was going on; right? Muslims and Croats and - Muslims and Croats only - are ordered to turn over all weapons, legal or illegally held; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a transcript of what was broadcast on Radio Sana of Sanski Most. It was read out. I cannot say whether Faik did this under duress. One cannot see whether he had a gun pointed at him. Now, speaking about the destruction of the town of Sanski Most, the town itself was not destroyed otherwise traces of that would have been visible. In 1993 I had an opportunity to pass through Sanski Most and I didn't see any major consequences of destruction --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Let me stop you. What about Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mahala was a significantly destroyed stronghold where houses were indeed devastated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this is after -- just after the operation we saw, Grmec 92, signed by the TO commander, was put in place. You said you didn't see anything in that operation that would suggest it was illegitimate. But what's being broadcast is for all the Muslim and Croat inhabitants only to turn over their weapons or their towns like Mahala will continue to be destroyed; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the order I did not see that any facilities were ordered to be destroyed unless they are being used for operations or if they were turned into strongholds. Reference here is made to the destruction of the town which definitely cannot be true because most of the inhabitants of the town were Serbs. Indiscriminate destruction of the town was impossible. No one would have had such an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not going back to the order, but it said to defend Serb neighbourhoods. Nobody is saying that Serb neighbourhoods were targeted by the 1 KK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go to page 7 in English, Serbian page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just under where it says "command of the Serbian armed forces," we see the female voice: "... all the struggle and retaliation will be in vain, you're not capable of standing up to the forces of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the statement of the Serbian armed forces command states. It adds, your resistance will force us to destroy and devastate your villages, which means that you will not be able to live with us in these territories. If you want to go on living in these territories, accept co-operation, hand over all the weapons and military equipment and surrender to the Serbian authorities all the extremists who force you to fight. As long as one of you has a weapon, you risk the destruction of your houses and families ..." That is exactly how the disarmament went in Sanski Most, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had accepted to be disarmed and did so, in the zone of the 1st Corps and in Sanski Most as well, were not exposed either to attacks or forcible disarmament. However, those who put up resistance and attacked the army certainly were subjected to disarmament with the use of military force and that there were casualties. So they had two choices: Either to surrender the weapon and wait for a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And what this says is that if the Serb armed forces -- if the VRS believes that not all weapons have been surrendered by the dead-line, they will shell the towns, the Muslim neighbourhoods; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it reads, but one knows very well what an ultimatum is. It is not an invention of the Serbian army, of the Serbian authority. In 1999, Serbia was given an ultimatum which it rejected and was subsequently attacked. This is a means which is generally accepted internationally but also in civil wars. Ultimatums are issued to the opposing side in order to avoid resorting to a different and more difficult solution for everybody involved. So one can abide by the ultimatum or not. They chose not to do it. They exposed themselves to operation, they became a legitimate military target. They were carrying out operations in this territory and one must always keep in mind that we are not speaking about the front line; we are speaking about the territory deep behind the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And we saw here that the call was to Muslim inhabitants, civilians, to surrender their legally and illegally owned weapons under threat of shelling. So are you considering that -- are you saying that's a legitimate ultimatum. If civilians keep some hunting rifles, the way the VRS can disarm them is by shelling their village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are emergency situations, and for that reason there are Crisis Staff in which it is possible that personal weapons for personal defence can be confiscated from citizens if the authorities deem that to be necessary. So if someone had something in possession, the authority had a right for them to be surrendered against a receipt and then to be returned to them once the conditions are in place. So we are not talking about something which was either legal or illegal. The situation was difficult, there were daily incidents in which the army or the police were attacked, and quite simply, the Serb forces were compelled to resort to forcible confiscation. But they were called up to submit and surrender that voluntarily and thus avoid such consequences. The destruction was not an outcome of the intention, but rather, an outcome of rejecting to accept certain authority in a certain area. And I'm not being specific about who I'm talking to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And yesterday you claimed that the disarmament operations were -- were ethnically neutral, that they were not aimed at just Muslims and Croats, but at everybody equally. There's nothing in anything we've seen, these Crisis Staff notes, in the broadcast, there is no hint anywhere that Serbs also must turn in their weapons. It's expressly directed at Muslims and Croats. Do you still say the 1 KK disarmed Sanski Most equally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying definitely that they equally treated everyone in Sanski Most who were possessing weapons illegally and for whom they knew that they had illegal weapons. We didn't see any documents, or rather, there were no available documents about the Serbs being in possession of these arms. But as far as the corps is concerned, when they issued their orders they never discriminate against any ethnic community. Rather, they said: Collect all illegal weapons from the population. And quite often they would use the phrase "irrespective of their ethnicity." This is what I spoke about. Now, how many Serbs were in illegal possession of fire-arms is a subject of another analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, during the break, if you have time, if you don't mind, I'd like you to look -- or point me to the 1 KK documents that say disarm, irrespective of ethnicity. If you can show me those because I must have missed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I go to P03928, please. This is footnoted in Mr. Brown's report at footnotes 340 and 452. And I want to look at who was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about the difficulties in performing triage and sorting out who is who. This is from the 15th of June. It's a MUP report from the chief in Sanski Most, Vrucinic, report on the process of disarming paramilitary formations in the Sanski Most SJB. And it begins: "Serbian army units and commands (six brigades), TO units, and SJB have for some time been disarming paramilitary Muslim and Croatian formations in the Sanski Most municipal area. "The action of peaceful disarming and surrendering of weapons was carried out in the period between 10 May and 25 May 1992. During that ... the Muslim and Croatian population handed over only hunting weapons and other legally owned weapons, but illegally obtained military weapons were not surrendered, and were concealed (buried) on instructions from above. "On 25 May 1992, this 'disarming' was followed by a military action (attack) against the down-town neighbourhood of Mahala, which resulted in the capture of 2.000 civilians, but no significant amount of weapons have been found because they had been concealed earlier ..." Now, first, we agree Mahala was a Muslim neighbourhood, right, and you already said it suffered significant destruction; right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing here talks about disarming Serbs or Serb paramilitaries, does it? That's a yes or no question, I think.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. There's no mention of Serbs here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So this operation which we were looking at, this is after the notes and the tape, 2.000 civilians captured. Is that -- sorry, capture 2.000 civilians. Do you still doubt that those diary entries which said capture civilians for exchange meant exactly what they said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When analysing this document, I made a comparison with another document which says - I think it's a military report - which says that of the 800 or 900 captives, there were 400 long-barrelled weapons found with them. And this is a significant amount of weapons. I'm not aware of any operation carried out by the army where the police acted as a service for taking in the captives and where the seized weapons were stocked. I don't know what the commander, or rather, what kind of information the police had since the police was not itself involved in this operation, or rather, was not leading this operation. But if you look at other documents as well, we can find that they did indeed find certain amount of weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to stop --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in my analysis, I wanted to know why 12 people were killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you because the question was if you -- do you still doubt that those diary entries which said capture civilians for exchange meant exactly what they said? That was the question, not how many weapons were found.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I said, that this was not an official policy of the Serbian authorities and that it's not contained in any of the documents issued by either the army or the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that it was not correctly noted "capture civilians for exchange," instead it should read "captured civilians be exchanged."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Last time I'm going to ask you this question. Do you still doubt - you haven't answered it - that when we saw "captured civilians for exchange," that that meant what it said, capture civilians and use them to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubts that that is what is written, but I have doubts that that was the actual intention and that it was implemented. I have never seen any documents that would confirm that. The notes does not give me enough ground to confirm yes, this is how it was going to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P02639, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But you agree with Mr. Karadzic's intervention that the passage in the diary said "captured civilians to be used for exchange"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we upload that document. Whether it said to capture civilians to be used -- to use for exchange or to be used for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That should be P03329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's actually 25th of May, Your Honour. Should be English e-court 33, Serbian 25. Yes, it says: "Captured civilians to be used for exchange." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P02639 [Realtime transcript read in error "P02369"], please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is cited in Mr. Brown's report, sir, at 171 and 460. It's a conclusion -- that's not the right -- 02639.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think the transcript is wrong, although I -- 02639 is what I said. That's right in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've seen this document before, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. This is the 4th of June, Crisis Staff conclusions in Sanski Most. Mirko Vrucinic, the chief of police; Nedeljko Rasula, president of the Crisis Staff; Nedjo Anicic, TO commander, "shall be in charge of resolving issues of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca." "1 ... politicians. "2 ... nationalist extremists. "3 ... people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality ... "In view of this, have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1 KK." The first question: Colonel Stevilovic is the security chief, right, at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One category I don't see here is combatants, another one I don't see is war criminals. In your view is it legitimate to deport politicians and people unwelcome to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that prisoners, regardless of for which category of population they come, all of those about whom, according to international conventions, one can say that they have the status of a prisoner of war, and it was my view that all those who were captured took part in combat or were related and involved in these operations in a certain way and that thus they can be afforded the status of prisoners of war. Now, as for this categorisation, saying that someone is a politician, that someone was an extremist, or that they were undesirable as a result of their conduct is an additional scheme of qualifications for which I found no grounds in the documents I reviewed. Now, back to the question of prisoners, I believe that all those who were taken prisoners should enjoy the status of prisoners of war. As for this, this was done on a different basis and by applying different criteria and this document doesn't show why they decided to divide them into these categories in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you're aware - and we'll get to them later - that there were complaints from Manjaca camp that many, many prisoners were being brought there who hadn't been involved in armed rebellions, who hadn't resisted the Serb authorities, who had simply been rounded up, who were simply civilians, and who were taken to Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. There were reports about that coming from the camp and these reports exist. It is true that at times civilians were held as well in this kind of prisoner centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And that would be people who Rasula, Anicic, and Vrucinic decided were unwelcome in Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume -- I mean, I don't assume, but at that time there was a decision that after being held temporarily, all prisoners of war would be transported to the POW camp Manjaca. That was the only POW camp in the area. All the others were remand centres, interrogation centres, or holding centres. So the municipality and the brigade did not have any resources to set up a camp there, so they sent everybody from Sanski Most to Manjaca. Obviously there were errors made in the process that certain civilians happened to find themselves in the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We just read a document from the MUP that said they had 2.000 civilians captured, and I'd forgot to follow-up -- ask you a follow-up question where you said you didn't know about the police being involved in civilians. You know as an expert in this case, don't you, that people captured -- Muslims captured in Sanski Most during the disarmament operation were held in the MUP station there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that. I think it's either the matter of translation or misunderstanding. I did not say that MUP was not involved. What I said was that it was not the police who spear-headed the operation of disarmament of paramilitary formations, or rather, those who possessed illegal weapons. So they did not lead those actions, but I added that the police premises were sometimes used to bring in those who were taken prisoners and these premises were under the MUP control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, this would be a good time, Your Honour, if we going to break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the outset of the hearing today I meant to ask Mr. Tieger when we would expect or we could see the response of the Prosecution to the accused's motion for suspension.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I actually intended to raise that on my own when we resumed at the break, but we are trying our best to expedite a response and get it back to you by close of business Friday or some point on late Friday. Again, if that -- I'm certain we'll be able to get it in obviously before Monday, but our intention at this point is to push hard to try to get it to the Court by Friday so that we can -- if the Court intends to have a hearing, as I understand it does, we can do so early in the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates the effort very much. Thank you. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. In 1992 when you were in the 1 KK, you were chief of security for the 1st Armoured Brigade, right, you told us that before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me read you part of your Mladic testimony when you testified here last month in that case, and just to orient you, this is concerning your trip to Nova Kasaba and Bratunac on the 17th of July, 1995, when you met and spoke with Zoran Malinic at Nova Kasaba. And he told you that on the 12th/13th of July they had taken 2500 civilians and soldiers prisoner. And you later testified about returning to the Main Staff where you were meant to report. And Judge Moloto asked you a question. This is at T 12890 in that case, and it was 18 June 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "Now, are you able to explain to us why you probably did not highlight that civilians were present," speaking about those captured in Nova Kasaba, "if you knew that keeping civilians as POWs is not permissible according to the law? "A. Well, as I conveyed that and the way in which I conveyed that, I really cannot recall now. And why I did not highlight it then and the form I put it in, I really have no recollection of that. "Judge Moloto: May I interrupt you? I'm not asking you to recollect anything. I'm asking you to give an explanation today why you did not highlight the fact that civilians were being taken amongst POWs if you knew at that time that civilians were not supposed to be taken as POWs? I'm asking for an explanation now. I'm not asking you to remember anything." Your answer: "The Geneva Conventions from 1949 is something I studied in detail only when I worked on certain findings in 2011 in relation to POW camps of the 5th Corps of the BH army. It was then that I found out unequivocally who can be a prisoner of war. At the time when all of this was happening, I did not have any reliable knowledge about that. Today," June 18th, 2013, "I know that civilians cannot be prisoners of war." That was your testimony in the Mladic case; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to Manjaca camp in 1992. Your report concentrates mostly on the issue of water-supply, that's at pages 90 to 94 of the English of your report; claims that it was difficult for everybody at Manjaca because of lack of food and difficult circumstances. I'd like to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me tell you and ask you if you know about this. You said you know of the Biscevic family in Sanski Most. There was a young man, a dentist, from Sanski Most named Edin Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is contained P00135 at e-court pages 88 to 89.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was also on that 7 July transport to Manjaca camp from Sanski Most. He was on a different truck. And the testimony we have in this case is that not all the prisoners were dead, some of them were very ill, or sick or suffering, from that confinement in the heat. And that the prison camp Manjaca would not take not just the dead prisoners but would not take the ones who were sick and who were dying. This young man, Edin, offered to try to help resuscitate and help the prisoners who were ill and dying, and the sick prisoners and the corpses were put on a truck along with Edin Biscevic and taken away. And Edin Biscevic was never seen again. Do you know about that, since you were involved with taking his twin brother out of Manjaca camp later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not come across those details in any of the documents when I prepared my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Forget the documents. You helped get his twin brother out of that Manjaca camp. Did you know about the living twin brother, the only surviving Biscevic son, did you hear or know about how for the twin brother of Nedim Biscevic, who you helped bring out of the camp, had disappeared?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'm not sure that I was the one who helped bring out Nedim Biscevic of the camp. I may have been a member of the commission who discharged somebody from the camp pursuant to somebody's decision. I was not the person in charge, I was not in a position to either bring somebody in or discharge somebody from the camp. I'm afraid I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, okay, sorry --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- much about the lot of his brother at the time. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you don't remember, you don't know. We'll get to it. But you testified at 40994 on direct here when you were shown D03843: "This was preceded by an order of the security chief of the 1 KK and I was one of its members at the time. And we went there, made this arrangement, and this person was eventually released from the camp," and that person was Nedim Biscevic. We'll get to that in a minute, but just to refresh your recollection. Now let me ask you this: When a truck of prisoners from Sanski Most arrives at Manjaca camp and the camp notices that 24 of those prisoners have died through maltreatment on the way there and that other prisoners are sick, dying, and need help, why does the camp give those sick, dying prisoners back to the people who put them in that condition in the first place? Why didn't your 1 KK camp take in those injured, sick prisoners and try to help them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about any specific reasons. I did not have at my disposal the complete documentation relative to the reception of these people. I know that a certain number of prisoners died during the transport. The assumption was that they had suffocated due to the lack of oxygen. I'm not aware of any other details. I'm not aware of the exact circumstances. I believe that so far I have not seen any document or heard that there were people who were still alive and were not allowed entry into the camp. This is completely new to me. I may have omitted that from the documents that I have perused, I may have missed that, actually. But this is the first time I hear that people were turned back even if they were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in 1992 you didn't know that civilians couldn't be prisoners of war, but you did know, didn't you, that it would have been the duty of the camp to try to assist those people if there were sick, ill people being brought to the door of the camp, prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a certain extent I was aware of the fact that civilians could not be prisoners of war. When I say "civilian," I mean any person who did not take part in combat or did not help combatants. However, what I said in the Mladic case was that it was only later that I studied the Geneva Conventions when I started dealing with that properly. I didn't know the details of who was supposed to be taken as a prisoner of war and who wasn't, but I knew that civilians were not among those who were supposed to be taken prisoner. But I knew that in any camp those who were still alive but wounded or in a bad state should have been administered help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But just again, what you testified to under oath in Mladic last month here when asked if you knew at the time - and that was July 1995 - that civilians were not supposed to be taken as POWs, your answer was: "It was then," 2011, "that I found out unequivocally who could be a prisoner of war. At the time when all of this was happening, I did not have any reliable knowledge about that. Today I know that civilians cannot be prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me go to 65 ter 25371, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing so, shall we ask the witness to excuse himself for a minute. We have something to discuss in your absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall I deal with an administrative matter. In assessing the accused's motion to admit documents previously marked for identification, filed on the 11th of July, 2013, the Chamber has noted an issue with one of the documents tendered in the motion, that is, MFI D3716. On the 19th and 20th of June, 2013, pages 4, 24, 25, 28, and 29 of the B/C/S original version of the MFI D3716 were discussed with Witness Bogdan Subotic and marked for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber notes that currently the entire B/C/S version of the document is uploaded into e-court and that the English translation does not correspond to the correct pages used with the witness. The Chamber therefore instructs the Defence to upload to e-court the accurate excerpts of the B/C/S original, as well as the corresponding English translation for MFI D3716 by Tuesday, 30th July 2013. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have 65 ter 25371, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Does that man look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot say. I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll look at the document again that Mr. Karadzic used on direct with you, which showed that this man was taken out of Manjaca camp and you said, again at T 04994 [sic], regarding that process: "This was preceded by an order of the security chief of the 1 KK and I was one of its members at the time and we went there, made this arrangement, and this person was eventually released from the camp." This is Edin Biscevic, who were talking about a little while ago - his brother Nedim - was taken away on July 7th from Manjaca camp and never seen again. His brother -- until this point his brother Haris was taken away and never seen again. Now, this is the Biscevic family you talked about. When you came to get him, did you know that his twin brother had been given up by the camp and put back on the truck by the people who brought those corpses to the camp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. As far as I can remember, I didn't see Nedim Biscevic then. We were in the camp as a commission. I think we signed a document, according to which the order of the 1st Corps chief of security was being implemented and Edin Biscevic was being released from the camp. And that was done then, that is what we confirmed. I don't even know if I went to the actual camp out of the administration building to see Nedim Biscevic. I confirmed the document and its authenticity, that I was in the commission that was implementing the order by the chief of security for that person to be released from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is that same person, right, Nedim Biscevic from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could see the document again, then I think -- yes, if it says "Nedim," then that's probably that. I said that I didn't recognise the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's bring up D03843, please. 3843 -- D, it's D, sorry, it's Mr. Karadzic's exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the document, right, Nedim Biscevic, son of Faik, so it's the same person; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 25371.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date here is the 17th of June. I don't know whether that refers to the date of the document, but at the top it should state "August" or this is something else. I don't want there to be any confusion. It should be the 26th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Handwritten thing is in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, if you look at the top left, Mr. Keserovic, it says "August 1992, 26th August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I don't see the point of admitting the article and the substance of it. The witness hasn't been able to confirm anything about this 2007 article, other than it's the same person. So I don't -- unless they just want to admit the photograph without the text, I don't see any basis for admitting the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, he's also confirmed it's the same person and that it's part of the same family that he knew of in Sanski Most. He didn't know that this person's -- that Nedim Biscevic's twin brother had been taken away and killed, but he was able to comment that this article concerns the same person that he took out of the camp. They're both sons of Faik Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that can't open the door to everything that the person later says just because it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So how is that article relevant to the Prosecution case? Are you tendering it for the credibility issue or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm tendering it to show that it's corroborative of the testimony in the case which is in the case by the father who is now deceased, Faik Biscevic, and it links the two brothers, the two -- twins. And the witness has corroborated the fact that this man was in Manjaca camp, which is what the article is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Faik Biscevic, who appeared in the radio broadcast transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, he's this man's father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have a basis to admit it. We'll assign a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6466, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Very quickly, again your testimony was that you were one of the members of this commission. We can see that on D03843. It was preceded by an order of the security chief, and that Vojo Kupresanin, president of the ARK Assembly, is the person who took over this prisoner, signed the document. Tell me how this worked. Why is a prisoner from Manjaca camp being taken over, with your involvement, by the president of the ARK Assembly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in the document it is not written, but the president of the ARK Assembly appeared - as far as I can remember - and it was said that he had the permission of President Karadzic or someone from the top Serbian leadership for that person to be released from the camp. In view of the fact that these were persons who were members of the army, this had to be co-ordinated with the security chief from the corps command who was Stevan Bogojevic at the time. So he issued an oral order for that person to be handed over to Mr. Kupresanin, and this is that record that the -- that Kupresanin took that person from the camp and took that person out of the camp. So I want to specify that I wasn't the one who took the person out of the camp because this is what was suggested to me in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And what did Vojo Kupresanin do with this former prisoner? Was he kept a prisoner, taken somewhere else and imprisoned again, or was he released? What happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my recollection, I think that he was released then and that he was not taken to any other camp or prison later. I don't know where he went afterwards --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it he wasn't a dangerous Green Beret killer or he wouldn't have just been released, right? He wasn't a war criminal, this dentist?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that was the reason that the authorities released him from the prisoner of war camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So let me just get it straight and then we'll move on. This man is arrested in Sanski Most, this dentist, during the disarmament operation. He's brought to Sanski Most on 7 July. His two brothers are murdered. And he's not released until the end of August 1992? Why does it take that long to release him if he's not a criminal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a reference where it was established that he did not take part in preparations for fighting or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- aided the fighting in some other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not a proper intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Nicholls --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is taking that as an established matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He asked the witness -- he asked the question. It's fair enough to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why does it take that long to release him if he shouldn't be there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure of reception and release of prisoners of war is set down. When this person was brought to the POW camp, together with the accompanying documentation, the list where his name was, was taken in and treated and considered as a prisoner of war by the camp administration. As for the period when certain categories of persons are identified as persons who should not be held any longer until the time they are released, that period is a relative thing because there are many questions that are posed there. At that time, it was simply not possible to take out Nedim Biscevic and say: You are free, you can go wherever you want. He wouldn't have had anywhere to go, so you had to create preconditions for some official organ, some humanitarian organisation or some other subject that had the possibility of unrestricted movement and passage to take that person together with the proper documentation. So it's really a relative thing as to how long it took for all of these conditions to be created. I would just like to add, there were others -- there were other categories - we have documents - other categories of persons who, because there was no longer any need for them to remain at the camp, were released. Some of them went abroad for medical treatment --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- religious officials were also released --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you because we're going to talk about releases and then you can explain. This doesn't give any category of why he's released, does it? Yes or no? It just says he's released.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he was a prisoner of war of that status. It does not say why he was released. It doesn't say that here, but you can see that he was released and that a representative of the government and the responsible command of the 1st Corps were also involved in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And what you said just a moment ago was he wouldn't have anywhere to go. He couldn't just go home to Sanski Most, could he, even if he was found to have been an improperly imprisoned civilian? Because they'd taken out -- they deported to Manjaca everybody unwelcome in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is oversimplifying things --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, you said he would have nowhere to go --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if you put it in that way --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said he would have nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't have anywhere to go. Manjaca is far away, not too far away, but it's far away from Sanski Most. There was no means for him to go or any place to go without the proper transport means. Public transport --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, sorry, let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was not functioning and there were no communications for him to be able to call anyone --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see what you're saying. You didn't say there was no bus, you didn't say he couldn't call a cab, you didn't say he couldn't hitchhike. You said he wouldn't have had anywhere to go.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had he been released without this procedure, he wouldn't know where to go and he wouldn't have anywhere to go. He could have just stayed in front of the camp. It was just that sort of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. At page 93 of your report you state that: "The fact that cases of unlawfulness which did occur were isolated cases committed by individuals acting on their own and without orders, such cases, as was the murder of Omer Filipovic, were investigated and documented. Today the perpetrators are still serving their prison sentences which were handed down by the Serb court and prosecutors." Now, you don't say "military court" there, you say "Serb court," and that's because the murderers of Omer Filipovic weren't tried in the Banja Luka military court, were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the final verdict was handed down a little bit later. I don't know which court it was that actually handed down the sentence. I would need to look at that. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me help you, it's the district court in Banja Luka, criminal case number K5/06, accused Zeljko Bulatovic, et cetera, et al., and it was in 2006.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you said: "The fact that in some cases even camp wardens -- even the camp warden was unable to control ordinary guards but such cases were eventually rectified through disciplinary and criminal sanctions against the offenders." So again, are you crediting the 1 KK preventing crime, disciplining offenders, prosecuting the guilty for a conviction in 2006 in a civilian court, over ten years after the war ended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not saying that the proceedings in 2006 were conducted thanks to the 1st Krajina Corps because it ceased to exist much earlier. What I am saying is that problems did exist, they were identified, and the camp administration did report to the corps command of those problems and the corps command in turn reacted and issued orders that measures be taken in respect of those who were behaving wilfully and committing the atrocities and crimes and misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
