utterances.text: Okay. Okay. You'd been to Manjaca camp. You were in the 1 KK in 1992. You tell me the name of one camp guard, one person working at the camp who was prosecuted in a military court during the period of the war, one.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not -- I don't know. I was there for a short period of time. I was at the Manjaca camp briefly, but -- and I was at the 1st Krajina Corps only until the 14th of September, with a break when I was on sick leave for over one month because I was wounded --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know. That's the answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You testified in the State Court in BiH, right, in April 2012?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was about camps run by the ABiH in which Serbs were kept in terrible conditions; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in that case - and I'm referring to 65 ter 25408, e-court pages 135 to 136 - you were asked by Defence counsel about how as an expert in that case you came to your findings. And you were asked: "Well, this claim of yours, expert, requires analysis. How did you determine that POWs were physically and mentally ill-treated? What proof do you have in that regard?" "You had said it was done by guards at the detention centres. How did you determine that, Mr. Keserovic, you included that in your report?" Your answer was: "Yes, I relied on the statements of the POWs." "Q. Thank you. How did you determine that other soldiers came to the detention centre and ill-treated the POWs? How did you determine that? "A. The same, based on documents in the case file. "Q. Did you use other types of evidence or did you rely on statements of POWs? "A. Well, for the most part I relied on the statements of POWs." So that in that case was a legitimate way for you to determine conditions in the camp and how prisoners were treated when you were talking in the state court about a camp run by the ABiH. In your report I don't see any reliance whatsoever on statements by prisoners in Manjaca camp; right? You didn't include that in your analysis for this Court here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents that were used by Mr. Brown and that I received from Mr. Karadzic's Defence, I included in this report or in these findings. I did not deny the bad, I can even say insufferable, unbearable conditions at the Manjaca camp. The only thing that I disputed was that this was the product of the intention of the camp command, the 1st Krajina Corps command, or of the authorities to keep people in such conditions. Therefore, I do not dispute that the conditions were difficult, that there were insufficient quantities of food, that there was a shortage of water and so on. But it was the best possible that could be provided at the camp at the time in those conditions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm not talking about conditions. That's where I started. I'm not talking about the water-supply. I'm talking about prisoners being savagely beaten. I can move on quickly if you'll say to me you don't dispute that prisoners in Manjaca were beaten -- terribly beaten by the guards there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases when prisoners were beaten, but that was not a rule and it was not permitted. I saw reports and statements about these cases when people were beaten. I'm not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just quickly go to P02972, please. I'm skipping ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, to save some time I'm not going to go through the documents, but you'll just agree with me that, just like Sanski Most, prisoners were brought to Manjaca from Kljuc municipality as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at what was going on in Kljuc. This is the Serbian Republic Ministry of the Interior Banja Luka Security Services Centre Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, P02972. I keep giving you the wrong numbers today. It is actually the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the 28th of September, 1992. Now, that's pretty late after things started in May. This is a strictly confidential official secret. It's the report on criminal offences committed in the municipality since the armed rebellion broke out on 27 May 1992. So this is a report on the situation from the end of May to the end of September. Take a time to look at it, because I want to go through it in a bit of detail. It starts off talking about how: "On 27 May 1992, Muslim extremists caused an armed rebellion," which resulted in three members of the Serbian army and police being killed and 30 members wounded. Then it goes on to say there have been 36 murders, 106 torchings and explosions, and 92 aggravated thefts and thefts. The next paragraph is what I want you to focus on. "These are officially reported indicators that do not reflect the actual situation because a large number of offences were not reported due to fear, the absence of an injured party, et cetera. In the first days of the war, this Organisational Unit independently established more than 140 break-ins, mostly on the premises of the territory of Kljuc and Sanica. "The start of war activities was characterised by break-ins of business premises and illegal entry into Muslim apartments by military persons. Then came a process of provoking fear and pressuring persons of Muslim nationality to move out by burning their houses, throwing explosive devices, firing Zoljas, /hand-held rocket-launchers/, and infantry weapons at apartment buildings. "In fact, it was commonplace to set fire to an entire hamlet of some 20 houses ... in a single night ..." This is the same period as the documents we were looking at and the tape for Sanski Most. The police here are reporting, aren't they, that there was a process by which the military are pressuring the Muslims to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that it was the army who was exerting pressure on the Muslims to leave. Here we have a summary report or information about criminal offences committed in the area of Kljuc municipality covering the period of about 40 -- four months. And in those four months, which were actually crucial months where significant events took place, this information is probably correct. When I looked at this document and evaluated it, I reached a conclusion that the incidents, or rather, offences had undoubtedly been committed, but that the majority of them -- it says here "military," which means member of the army because according to the law, military personnel refers only to commissioned officers that have ranks, but in this particular instance they probably referred to all members of the military. As I said, a large majority of these incidents in which people were victimised and where there were torching and looting was probably a reaction to numerous incidents committed by Muslims and Croats during or around this period, or rather, by the 27th of May or thereabouts. Military columns were attacked, police were attacked, there were instances of capture. So there were a lot of casualties --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, let me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this information that over the four months the number of the killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, this talks about casualties and the rebellion of -- three members of the Serbian army and police were killed and 30 wounded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, this information is not correct. More members of the army than three were killed. Seven members were killed in a single incident. They were passing by unarmed in a column and they came across an ambush and that is where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to skip over the part about the serious crimes, the murders, the killing with hammers, et cetera. Go to the next page in the English, where it does say at the top - and I think we need to go to the next page in the witness's version as well - it does say that: "Recently, there have been actions of revenge in reaction to soldiers being killed at the front. As a result, five people were killed in their homes in Sanica." But I want you to look at this part: "Through operative work, information has been obtained that the perpetrators are persons in uniform, that is, military persons who do not fall under the jurisdiction of the SJB. However, due to war conditions, the military security organs have only seldom discovered perpetrators and they sanction such crimes by sending them to the front line. These crimes are being reported to the station, which simply does not know how to deal with them." Now, that's exactly right, isn't it? The Court's seen documentation here that instead of prosecuting members of the army who committed crimes, they were released from custody and sent to the front. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases, and one of the measures was to dispatch them to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me look at another document with you quickly. And this goes to your --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I have about ten minutes of the three and a half hours I'd planned. I'm going to ask you for some more time. The reasons I would give are, first of all, that Mr. Karadzic, when you made your assessment, Mr. Karadzic had listed one hour for the witness and used 4.5 hours on direct. And the second reason is there is a brief period where the witness will recall he went down to Nova Kasaba and Bratunac on 17 July 1995 at the order of General Mladic and I'd like to ask him a couple questions about that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About the schedule, then, we'll not hear Mr. Savcic this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think the -- given the length of the re-direct examination and the fact that we have to start with another witness on Monday, there wouldn't be much point in calling him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what would the schedule -- witness schedule be like for next week? Djuric and Kos has a specific date, Monday and Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well -- yes. Djuric will testify first thing Monday morning and then General Savcic will testify right after him. Then we will probably have the videolink on Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- which may have to interrupt General Savcic's testimony. And when that's over, either General Savcic will finish or then Kos will resume and then we have two other witnesses for the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the name of the videolink testimony witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Kljajic, Cedomir Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was fixed for Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, trying to move quickly, I'm going to move to the issue of the moving out of the population and real property, apartments, et cetera. That's at Brown's report primarily at pages 110 to 122, paragraphs 2.134 to 2.163; and your report at pages 48 to 49, paragraph 25. And you stated on your direct at 40959, that Mr. Brown made an error of law in terms of the laws that were in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time and he put an equation mark between ownership and tenancy rights which is not the same, far from it. And then you talked about socially owned flats where the flats were owned by companies, et cetera. And you ended up saying in this section: "As a result in his report he says that upon departure of the Croats and Muslims, their flats were confiscated and given to be used by someone else. This was simply something that was stemming from the law in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time." And you give an example in your report at page 49 of the English, where you analyse document P03642.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in your report - and this is cited as footnote 51 in your report - you quote into your report: "Decision on the criteria for the possibility of departure from the Kljuc municipality" --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. P03462, I apologise. P03462.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then you quote the beginning of Article 2: "Permanent departure from the territory of the municipality shall be allowed to persons who have exchanged their real property, houses, and land or privately owned apartments with persons from areas to which they are moving." That's all you quote from the document. And then you say: "It is evident from this document that permanent removal was possible only if people leaving had exchanged their property ..." Let's look at the whole document. This is the 30th of July, 1992, the War Presidency of Kljuc municipality adopted the following decision. Article 1, which you didn't include, people may move out, "declaring that they are moving permanently from the territory of Kljuc municipality, shall be permitted to leave the territory voluntarily." And then we see Article 2 which you quoted the parts about exchange. And then there's a part you left out. "The exchange of real estate must be carried out in advance of, or at the latest, three months after moving out; otherwise, any real estate shall be taken over by Kljuc Municipality." And another part you left out: "Persons who place their real estate at the disposal of Kljuc Municipality shall also be permitted to move away permanently from Kljuc Municipality." So when you say it's evident from this document that permanent removal was possible only if people leaving had exchanged their property, that's just not correct on the face of the document, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, further on it is correctly stated that they are not obliged to do the exchange if they leave a written document stating that they place their property to the municipality for disposal. So they had to resolve the issue of their private ownership in a way. That was the intention behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That may have been your intention, but it's not what your report says. What your report says: "It is evident from this document that permanent removal was possible only if people leaving had exchanged their property ..." And that's not true. You just said it's not true. People will be allowed to leave permanently - this is Kljuc where we just saw how whole hamlets were torched in one night - if they leave their property to the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible, just as is stated in Article 2, either through exchange or by leaving it at disposal. Should they fail to do either, within three months the property would be inventoried and would definitely be placed at the disposal of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You just said "either"; your report says "only." You were trying to make it look in your report as though the only way people would leave permanently was if there was a consensual exchange and that's not true, is it? If a person can't exchange their property, Kljuc takes it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the procedure. The local commune, or rather, the municipality is the one who disposes of the entire stock of real property in its area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and that has nothing to do with socially owned housing and apartments which you tried to portray this as earlier, because Article 3 talks about socially owned apartments in a separate category; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show a couple other documents to you. P03517. This is dated 21st September 1992, back to Sanski Most. "Ana Stojic is hereby permitted to move permanently out of Sanski Most municipal area towards Novska - Croatia ... with the following members." Did you know that Grgo Stojic survived an execution in Skrljevica in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You didn't know that he was shot by Danilusko Kajtez, who was a member of the SOS and the 6th Krajina Brigade, shot at -- with two other accomplices?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know people who were victims by name, but I do know about Danilusko Kajtez who committed crimes and I know that he was tried for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, after the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure whether it was after the war. I think that he was arrested immediately after these events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to go through the whole Kajtez story with you; there's evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P06439.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from Novi, similar, 9 July, regarding the statement of the person present about his property for the purpose of permanently leaving the municipality. Persons present, person concerned. And the statement is: "I have no fixed assets in my name in the Municipality of Bosanski Novi and I am leaving the municipality of Bosanski Novi permanently." Did you know that Midho Alic saw his brother murdered and he was detained at the Bosanski Novi stadium?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know who this Alic person is, honestly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For people like Grgo Stojic and Midho Alic who have been the victims of crimes, would you consider their leaving under these circumstances voluntary, regardless of what these certificates say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already said - and I'm stating that in my report - that the state of general insecurity and the general conditions were the strongest factor that contributed to the process of moving out. Had everything been all right and well, I'm sure that wouldn't have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, back to Manjaca for just a couple questions. In your report, you're critical in your paragraph 52 of Ewan Brown's report. At 2.132, Mr. Brown said: "It would appear that the military made no attempt to let those prisoners," from Manjaca, "go back to their homes. Furthermore, the destruction and fear created by the Serb army, police, and authorities would probably have made it impossible for them to go home, even if they had wanted to. As a result, all the prisoners were escorted out of the territory under intense pressure." And you say there are no grounds for such a conclusion and that his paragraphs are full of contradictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P03723, please. Which has to be confidential, Your Honours, I'm sorry, for the same reasons which we've discussed and this may need to be decided later, but if we could use the same procedure for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified before in this Tribunal in the Blagojevic, Tolimir, and Mladic cases; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, I'm sorry, could we take the break early, and outside the witness I have something very brief to ask Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll do so. General Keserovic, we'll have a break. We'll resume probably at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session -- no, sorry, we don't need -- sorry, I'm tired. We deferred before the question of advising the witness of his rights under Rule 90. I'm now going to talk about the witness's -- briefly talk about the witness's trip to Srebrenica, to the Bratunac-Nova Kasaba area on 17 July 1995. I'm going to show him a document in which General Mladic puts him in charge of a sweep operation which may be linked to executions of prisoners found in the Cerska mass grave. That's where I'll be going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know, Your Excellency, is the procedure the same if we have an expert witness or a witness on facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I could just say, Your Honour, sorry to interrupt you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to turn to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He's been given the warning before, and I'm going to now be asking him questions as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I think the warning -- it would be better to give the warning since it was given before when he testified about the same topics. Secondly, we may have had some basis to object about turning an expert witness into a fact witness, but in principle we don't object because it could be relevant to his credibility. But we also think that it will open the door for us to use information about the Srebrenica events or to elicit information about the Srebrenica events from General Keserovic, who we hadn't previously called as a fact witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I would just say there that there would be no objection, since he's testified three times before about this -- the Srebrenica events. The fact that they call a fact witness who was a participant doesn't prevent us from asking evidence which advances our case or impeaches his credibility. And it sounds like Mr. Robinson is trying to say the floodgates will be open to any questions they wish to put on re-direct when they chose not to call him as a fact witness or put any questions on direct. So I accept that he will have the normal re-direct of questions that arise out of my cross-examination, but that me asking him now anything about his role in Srebrenica does not open the doors to them doing a direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you agree with Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't, actually, but maybe it's better to see how it goes. But since we decided not to -- it would have not been proper for us to elicit fact evidence from an expert witness. So once the -- his role in the facts of the case are open, then we think it's a different situation than simply the scope of re-examination -- or re-direct examination for a fact witness, for someone who was here as a fact witness from the beginning. But maybe the cross-examination will be broad enough that it won't really arise in a concrete way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just from a legal point of view that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we leave it there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we are to follow your suggestion, Mr. Robinson, then the Prosecution should be entitled to another cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I would think they would on matters that were raised for the first time in our re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There's no legal foundation for that whatsoever. There's no prohibition from them calling him in part as a fact witness and in part as an expert, and choosing to call him solely as an expert witness doesn't change anything about my cross-examination and the normal scope of re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the reason you are objecting to such a scenario is the lack of notice as a fact witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that and it's just improper because the fact that I'm now going to cross-examine him on a narrow topic doesn't change anything. They knew he was a fact witness when they called him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But can they not call him later on as a fact witness later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They can call him later on as a fact witness, but then we need a witness statement or a 65 ter summary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the point of your objection is the matter of notice. If you're ready, there's no reason for you to object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it's more procedural. If they want to call him as a fact witness, that's fine. If they want to do it as a fact witness, then I won't cross him on it now. We can just stop and he can go to his re-direct right now. They can call him as a fact witness about Srebrenica and then I'll cross him on whatever he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you want to add anything, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, the Prosecutor objected when I asked General Radinovic about facts as a fact witness and the Trial Chamber sustained that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because you didn't notify the parties that you are going to ask him factual questions. But let's -- let's come back to this -- this issue, if necessary, after having heard the cross-examination. We'll have a break and we'll resume at 20 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, Mr. Nicholls informed me he was going to ask some factual questions to you not as an expert but as a fact witness about what happened in Srebrenica, et cetera. So in this regard, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). As you may be well aware of it, under this Rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Nicholls or later on Mr. -- the accused or even from the Judges if you believe your answer will -- might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used for -- in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have told you, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. On 16 July 1995 you arrived at the headquarters of the Main Staff; right? You said that in Mladic last month.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you came from the western part of the theatre - you said that in Mladic last month - right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you could talk about what they said later, but that evening you saw General Miletic there in the operations room; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure and that's what I stated. I'm not sure whether I saw General Miletic that evening or the evening after, whether I saw him on the evening when I arrived at the Main Staff or the evening after that. This still remains a question which I cannot answer, i.e., I cannot confirm with certainty that it was either on the 16th, in the evening, or the 17th in the evening. All I know is that it was indeed in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And also same thing, you saw General Tolimir there? Your response would be the same but you saw General Tolimir as well; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P04588, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've seen this document before lots of times; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. It's from General Mladic, it's his order; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's dated 17 July 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's to the Drina Corps command for information, to the Zvornik Brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, and the 67th Communications Regiment; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion - I don't know whether it was in the Mladic case - we analysed the telegram in detail, to see who it was sent to. I believe that it was sent for the information of the Drina Corps, that it is possible, and that the other units received it directly. We did not get to the bottom of the thing as to who received it only for their information and who had to receive it to act on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: That's who we see on the top, the units it's directed to; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's headed: "Integration of operations to crush lagging Muslim forces. "Order," right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At paragraph 1: "Send three officers (Colonels Nedjo Trkulja, Milovan Stankovic, and Bogdan Sladojevic) from the Main Staff ... to the command of the Zvornik Brigade to assist in the joining of the VRS and MUP interior forces -- MUP forces, the planning and co-ordination of combat operations to block, crush and destroy lagging Muslim forces in the wider areas of Kamenica and Cerska." Now, Colonels Trkulja, Stankovic and Sladojevic indeed went down to Zvornik, didn't they, on the basis of this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they left; however, the documents that I have seen in the meantime indicate that that was indeed the case. So we can confirm that they did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And let's look at paragraph 2 -- 3, excuse me. "As of 17 July, the forces of the 1st blpbr, the 1st mlpbr, the 67th pv /military police/ battalion, 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, and MUP forces engaged in the wider areas of Bratunac, Milici, and Drinjaca will comb the territory in the zone of Bratunac-Drinjaca-Milici-Besici village with the aim of discovering and destroying lagging Muslim groups. I hereby appoint Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic, the officer for military police in the General Staff VRS security administration, as the commander of all the aforementioned forces during the conduct of the aforementioned task. The dead-line for the completion of this task shall be 19 July 1995, at 20 hours ..." And I'll talk about it a bit more, but this order, the written order puts you in command of those forces, combined forces, for this sweep operation; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can see that this was received by Milici on the 18th; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, judging by the stamp at the bottom of the page, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And P05097, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Another document I want to show you quickly. Now, you've seen this order from the commander of the special police, Goran Saric before as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was shown this document in one of the cases in which I testified, perhaps even in the Mladic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the answer's yes, you've seen it before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And this order from 17 July - I won't read out the distribution list - says to: "Urgently form a combat group the size of a battalion in the Kravica-Konjevic Polje sector ..." It lists the units: "Doboj special police detachment, two companies from," it says "the seminar on Jahorina, two PJP companies in order to search the terrain in the Pobudje sector in the course of today, 17 July 1995, and fully mop-up the right side of the Milici-Drinjaca road, before regrouping the search for Cerska." Now, you testified last month in the Mladic case that this MUP order by Goran Saric covers the same area and territory as General Mladic's order which lists you as commander, right, same area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is even the same time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And it puts Borovcanin as commander for these combat groups; right ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, General Mladic also, when you met him, gave you this same order orally, didn't he, before this written order was drafted? Basically the same order. You testified to that last month as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe not all of the elements, but he told me verbally and he told me that General Miletic would follow-up with a written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And let me just read part of your testimony to you, this is from last month when you testified in the Mladic trial, this is at T 12841: "Q. If you could tell us what unit you were supposed to be commanding according to what General Mladic told you?" And you said: "If I remember well, there were parts of different units of the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, the Communications Regiment, the Engineering Regiment of the 5th Corps, part of the military police battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, parts of -- or, rather, some units of the MUP, parts of the special brigade, and parts of the special and regular police units as well as engineering battalion of the Drina Corps." That testimony was truthful, right, that's what you remember the units Mladic telling you were going to be involved in this operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned these units based on the document, this one and some other documents that showed which of the units participated in the action, i.e., which were deployed in the area. I'm not sure that General Mladic gave me all of their names. He said that he would be in charge of scouring the terrain and that he would unify all of the units in the area, and that the operation would take place on the right bank of the Drinjaca and on the road leading from Milici to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just -- I won't read your answer again but let me read the question again you gave that answer to. "Q. If you could tell us what unit you were supposed to be commanding according to what General Mladic told you?" And you testified later, if it helps you, that what Mladic told you corresponded to the written order.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I stick by that answer. Those were the units. There were no others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Now, you claim you did not carry out this order because this written order we see was orally amended. Just please answer yes or no, and then I'll go over what you said about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What you said was: "I tried immediately to tell General Mladic, the commander of the Main Staff" -- I'm sorry this is at T 12846 in the Mladic testimony, "commander of the Main Staff, that as far as I was concerned this was a militarily unacceptable assignment and that there were many reasons why I should not execute it. It's true that General Mladic, in the way that he usually does, said, "Never mind, Miletic will explain everything." He turned and left the room. Then General Tolimir appeared or maybe he was already there. And then with General Tolimir and General Miletic, I tried to clarify this new situation that I found myself in. And as my superior officer, I asked General Tolimir to try to see if he could get a correction or a change of this order from General Mladic which, as I said, as far as I was concerned was militarily unacceptable." Do you stand by that testimony last month?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say that I shouldn't or that I mustn't. I said that I didn't have to or I couldn't. I'm not sure that I said that I mustn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me read out your explanation about what happened next. This is at T 12848. "Q. So now what happens? You complained to Mladic, Tolimir gets involved, it's still the evening of that -- let's call it your first night there. What happens? "A. General Mladic left and then after the conversation General Tolimir followed him out. He told me there that he would try and see what he could do about this. After a certain period of time, perhaps a couple of hours, General Tolimir returned and told me that General Mladic agreed that I should not take over command of those units but that I should go to the area where the operation was being carried out the following day, go to Colonel Blagojevic, gather information about what was being done and how it was being done and report about it when I came back." Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then you were asked this question: "So if you weren't going to be commanding these forces, who were you told that the Main Staff was commanding these forces? Clearly you must have had to report to them, I would guess. Is that right? Who got saddled with this job? "A. The job was not given to anyone. Again, Colonel Blagojevic continued with his assignment. I really don't know if somebody else later took over the assignment, but Blagojevic was the one who began to implement the task and he continued with it." So you stand by that, the job was not given to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, nobody was given that assignment. On that day, Blagojevic continued to work on the implementation of that task, at least when I was there in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And then Judge Orie questioned you about this at T 12853 last month and said: "So therefore, what do I understand, that the order or the assignment was given to you was, let me say it friendly, totally idiotic. Is that more or less what you're telling me? I mean, you don't get the means, you don't have the troops, you have nothing, and someone asked you to do a job. That is pretty strange, isn't it?" And your answer: "That's how it was." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my reply as to how the task was given to me and why I found it unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And you are not able to show us, and neither is anybody else, another written order from General Mladic or anybody else saying that Blagojevic or another person is commanding those units; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an order which precedes this one, where that assignment was given to Colonel Blagojevic and he was the one who was in charge. That document was shown to me during my testimony. I don't know whether it was issued on the 14th or the 15th of July. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm talking about anything after the 17 July order we just looked at that puts you in charge.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only aware of this order and what was shown to me with regard to the MUP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So this order gets sent out to the Milici units. We can see that. And there's no written order sent out to tell them that it's actually wrong, that you're not in command, so they don't know who's commanding and co-ordinating the sweep, right? There's nothing written sent to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How they were informed about that as to how to proceed and how to implement their tasks and whether they were informed about that in the first place, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And here's what you said your new job was after this oral amendment of the order. You said: "I should not take over command of those units but that I should go to the area where the operation was being carried out the following day, go to Colonel Blagojevic, gather information about what was being done and how it was being done and report about it when I came back." You stand by that, that was your new assignment; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one part of that new assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To go the area where these operations were taking place, observe, do nothing, command no one, and then report back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said it precisely. It was to go to see Colonel Blagojevic and get informed what was going on, not to go to the area where the operations were taking place and to observe what was going on myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Isn't Colonel -- isn't Blagojevic perfectly capable of reporting what's going on through the normal chain of command which works every single day in the Drina Corps, whereby he reports to his Drina Corps commander, General Krstic, and then they report to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could and I suppose that's how things functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And then the day after receiving this order, the next morning you went down to the area and you saw Zoran Malinic at Nova Kasaba at the side of the road; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to remind us, Zoran Malinic is commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Unit; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He's under the command of Milomir Savcic; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'll just go through this very quickly. Malinic told you at that time that on the 12th or 13th July -- well, strike that. Let me -- let me just read out what you testified that he said to you when you were testifying here last month in the Mladic case. This is at T 12863. "Q. Did he tell you about any prisoners on earlier days? "A. He did. He said that at the stadium in Nova Kasaba in his assessment there were between 2.000 and 3.000 -- or, I think he said 2500 captured and disarmed Muslims -- actually, fighters and civilians from Srebrenica who had been coming along the road between Kasaba and Konjevic Polje. "Q. And did he tell you anything about what he was doing with those prisoners. "A. Yes. He said that he had organised a process of registering -- of making lists of those prisoners. He also said that at some point in time he was interrupted when the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, came along. He stopped with his vehicle near the football-pitch, he assembled the prisoners and addressed them." Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is according to my best recollection of what I heard and what I remember from that time. This is something that I said for the first time to Jean Rene Ruez, and this question is always present. And I think that is what I remember, what I could remember, what I told Jean Rene Ruez in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at T 12865 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, were the interpreters provided with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but it is in e-court, we can bring it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be slow. I think they will be benefitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- by having that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the reminder. This is from T 12865.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were asked to confirm that and you were read back part of your Tolimir testimony, speaking of Zoran Malinic. "'He told me that his initial assignment was to register them, which he had started doing, he had started registering them, but he had to stop doing that because General Mladic told him to stop.' "Do you stand by that testimony you gave under oath?" Your answer was: "Yes." Do you still stand by it today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that is that testimony and I think that that is what I said, or rather, I stand by the statements I gave each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at some point after that on this trip you go to Bratunac; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you testified to this in Mladic at 12873 last month, and you were with Colonel Jankovic from the Main Staff at this point. "In addition to that, at one moment we stopped at the public security station in Bratunac. I don't know exactly why but Jankovic had some commitment there. I already said that at that public security station I came across Ljubisa Borovcanin, who was there in the field." Do you stand by that testimony, you ran into Borovcanin at the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then you were asked at the same page: "And was he involved in this sweep operation?" And you answered: "Yes. I learned that units of the MUP, especially members of the special brigade, were carrying out the task of searching the terrain within the area of this operation." Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that I found that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the written order that we saw from General Mladic put you in charge on the VRS side of this sweep operation. The written order by Goran Saric, the commander of the special police that we saw put Borovcanin in charge of the MUP units in the sweep operation, both signed on the 17th -- both issued for the 17th. And your testimony that you coincidentally happened to run into Borovcanin in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P05389. Sorry, a better one is P05390 [Realtime transcript read in error "P05380"]. This is from the 17th of July at 11.15 a.m. It's 90 I said, I believe, Your Honours. 05390.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, this is the 17th of July, we can see it on the print-out on the other version. We see a little further down: "Y: Has Keserovic set out already? "X: We came across him on our way here and he hasn't arrived here yet. "Well, he must have gone first forward over there to Momir Nikolic. "Uh-huh. "Let me tell you I just spoke a little while ago to General Miletic. "Okay. "He told me that Keserovic also has to come up here to solve these issues. "Yes ..." And then it talks a bit more about Salapura and Kovac speaking about a shift arriving. Now, General Miletic has a nickname -- sometimes used Mico, right, on the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't know that? This intercept 17 July shows that somebody's expecting you to come and resolve some issues, doesn't it, in the area apparently around Bratunac since it refers to Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not go to Momir Nikolic, but I stopped to speak with Malinic. Malinic was the first in the rank of the units. I also went to Blagojevic. I did not -- I did not even know Momir Nikolic, so -- and I did not go to him. I went to Blagojevic and they were in the same unit, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me read you back another question and answer from the Mladic case from last month, 12969. And it was in relation to an ICRC dispatch about missing people. "Q. Were you aware of it on the 17th of July as well, all the missing men from Srebrenica referred to here? "A. No. The day that I was in Bratunac I didn't know anything about it." You stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me tell you about a little bit of the testimony in this case. This is the testimony of Dusan Janc, 28 March 2012, T 27043 to 27045. On cross-examination by Mr. Karadzic, he explained how he determined that the Cerska executions took place, he says, sometimes later than the 13th of July. I would say around 17 July. And he explained that that was because four individuals who were noted as being alive after the 13th were found in the Cerska primary grave. And let me read out to you now something else from your Mladic testimony at 12982. "Q. Okay, General. Let me just get right to the point, that the indictment in this case has charged that sweep operation on the 17th captured over a hundred people and that they were summarily executed and buried in the Cerska valley. Had you been in command of those forces that did that sweep operation, would you bear any responsibility for the deaths of people captured in that?" And your answer was: "Certainly, it would be the responsibility of the operations commander, the person who carried out the executions." You stand by that statement; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me show you one more document, P05152. This is a dispatch from the Zvornik CJB, from the chief of that centre, Dragomir Vasic. And he says: "The RS MUP, /special police detachment/, and PJP /special police unit/ combed the terrain on the right of the Milici-Drinjaca road, including features behind Cerska and Udrc in order to liquidate the remnants of infiltrated groups from Srebrenica. The action was completed very successfully." So, sir, you have to say that the order putting you in charge of the military -- the VRS in the sweep operation was orally amended, don't you, because you agree that the commander of that operation ought to be liable for those executions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The question is: You have to say that written order was orally amended even though there's no written amendment and no other evidence in writing that it was amended, because you've already agreed that whoever was in charge of the VRS in that operation would be responsible for those executions? You said: "Certainly, it would be the responsibility of the operations commander and the person who carried out the executions."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the view that the commander is responsible for those who did carry out the executions, but there's no reason that I have to say it. It's simply how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing further at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Pursuant to Rule 90(H)(ii), I would request that the Chamber order the Prosecution to put their case to the witness on this subject. I think they're required to do that. First of all, is it their case that the executions in Cerska took place on the 17th of July, not the 13th, as they previously alleged? And secondly, is it their case that General Keserovic is responsible for that crime? I think that has to be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, the first thing I would say is hearing from this Defence team about the obligation to put your case is almost laughably incredible. They never put their case. Mr. Robinson stood up the other day when he was asked to put his case about whether they were executions in Branjevo and said: We reserve the right to take any position at any time, basically. Second, if I go back to his question, the -- this is not the first time that we've talked about the executions in Cerska being likely later. They are listed as on or about the 13th, something like that, in the indictment. We made it clear in our pre-trial brief at paragraph 241, it says there: "At some point between 13 and 17 July ..." So yes, the evidence -- there is evidence to support that these were done -- these executions took place on the 17th, and that came out of Mr. Janc during Mr. Karadzic's cross. And our case on Mr. Keserovic is just what I've put, that this document assigns him as commander and that we haven't seen -- that that is the evidence, that document assigns him as commander of these units. He's given his explanation that it was orally amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think General Keserovic should be given the chance to comment on that case if he believes there's something he would like to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. I thought I did give him that option with my last questions where I said this is the explanation that you've given and you've got to give because of the written order, but he can add anything he likes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I -- the witness has answered sufficiently, but if you'd like to add anything, Mr. Keserovic, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just want to say that really as far as the events in the Cerska valley are concerned, I don't know anything about that. I was never there myself nor do I know of this, so that I don't know that this happened. I saw some documents here and I know that graves were found in the Cerska valley, but I don't know what the events were and what the connection is there either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. But before I forget, the -- those documents put under seal, we'll leave it as they are -- as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, during the cross-examination you emphasised that you do not dispute the existence of crimes but that the focus of your attention was on the position of the authorities in relation to the events, to the occurrences; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 916, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The special focus of the cross-examination were to municipalities Kljuc, Sanski Most, and then a little bit of Kotor Varos as well, so I just would like us to see what we have there. Can you please tell us what is it -- this thing here, Crisis Staff -- command of the defence of Kljuc and the Crisis Staff, what is it warning about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are warning about an end to the incidents, namely, attacks on the army and the police in Kljuc because in that case there would be a response to those incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how does this fit into what you know about whether the authorities were giving an opportunity for a peaceful resolution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did emphasise that and continue to emphasise that there were first calls to a peaceful solution, then disarmament, surrendering of weapons, that an opportunity was given for all disagreements to be resolved in future, at some future time, through political negotiations, namely, that there was a chance for the conflict not to occur at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3898, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 867 now, please. And can we zoom in on the Serbian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, General, this is a meeting of the War Presidency of Kljuc on the 7th of August. So could you please look at paragraph 1 and could you please look at these three bullet points: "All institutions ... should take an active role ..." What is the War Presidency asking for here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all structures on -- in the area of the municipality, the command of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade, public security station, and the SDS should take an active role in preventing the destruction and demolition of family houses, that security organs and the military police should become active in arresting individuals and taking appropriate measures, that the Serbian Democratic Party should try to appeal to the people to stop hostilities in the municipality and to try to pull out heavy weapons to the brigade warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what sort of hostilities were there in the territory of the municipality, between who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hostilities in the Kljuc municipality were between the paramilitary formations, or rather, armed formations of the Muslims, dominantly, and to a part also of Croatian ones, and Serbian units and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3899, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When we're on this subject, could we look at the document shown to you by Mr. Nicholls from Kljuc also, that is P02972. Can you please tell us how this Vinko Kondic as chief of the public security station is treating these killings, or rather, these acts? How does he qualify these crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does it state here, second paragraph, line 4: "Monstrous occurrences and monstrous crimes took place, such as the killing of four Muslim persons ..." and so on and so forth. How does this fit into your position that there were crimes and what was the attitude of the authorities and how does this chief of police qualify that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He qualifies this in the way that it actually happened. He's submitting a report about the events and is not concealing anything. He's reporting here that these events did occur without any intention of glossing over anything or concealing anything in the municipality. And he's probably aware that this should not and ought not to have happened and measures are being taken in order to resolve these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In all fairness, given that answer and the question, how is the chief of public security station treating these crimes, the second-to-last paragraph should be put to the witness, where the police chief says exactly how he's treating these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at the penultimate paragraph and to tell us if this paragraph reflects an intention to suspend prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. It is only describing the reasons that were valid at the time for not filing criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 862.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. It's a document produced by the municipality which states, or rather, whereby it is banned to use and to dispose of private and socially owned property. Now, can you tell me what is the difference between disposing of or possessing and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic please repeat the last part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Interpreters were not able to hear your question in full. Could you repeat your last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My first question was: Is there a difference between disposing of and possessing something? And my second question was whether if someone is still in situ, hadn't moved out, do the authorities have the right to confiscate or commandeer property for waging the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Temporary disposal is temporary, as it says, and it is in force for as long as there is a need for that. Ownership of property is something that is of a permanent nature. Your second question relating to the possibility for both private assets and socially owned assets being commandeered, according to the Law on Defence, it is provided that both movable and immovable assets can be mobilised or commandeered for waging a war or more specifically for defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a news bulletin for Radio Kljuc. Look at the last paragraph and can you tell us what kind of report they received from the civil defence staff and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, problems relating to convoys of those people who were moving out are described here. These people were moving into different areas; however, they failed to reach an agreement probably about an unhindered passage and the reception of these people in different areas, most likely different countries, and the Red Cross and the civilian defence staff were involved in this entire procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this a story that was broadcast on the radio indicative of a postponement, and does that indicate that there was forcible expulsion in question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And please put a pause before you start answering the question. Your answer always overlaps with the interpretation of Mr. Karadzic's words in interpretation. Will you reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what arrangements were made and how these convoys were organised? According to what you know, were there any forcible expulsions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documents accessible to me, it was permanently highlight that no pressure should be exerted or any forcible moving out of any individual who wanted to leave the area. The relocation was carried out in the following way: Those who were interested in leaving had to report, and upon a number of individuals were compiled in a list, then a convoy would be arranged to take them to the destination that they were interested in going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just clarify this, were they physically gathered or did you mean lists?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not gathered physically. Most often they would report to the Red Cross or an office that was in charge of these issues, where they would be listed. Once the conditions were in place for relocation, they would be notified, and that is how their relocation was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this particular document what are they being notified of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document they're being notified of the fact that they would not set off at 9.00, as originally planned, because not all the agreements had been reached with regard to their departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3900, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have a look at P3448.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a Prosecution exhibit in evidence which is helpful to all concerned. Can you tell us how does this statement or public announcement fit to what you just explained to us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the way how the departure of citizens who wanted to move out was put into practice, and then in paragraph 3 it is stipulated that the civilian protection should be in charge of this implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 790.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on the 5th of May, what was the Kljuc municipality Crisis Staff appealing? Can you please just summarise these four bullet points that we see in the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an appeal to all citizens in the municipality to preserve the public order and peace, not to jeopardise the safety and security of individuals and their property, to familiarise themselves with an order on disarmament that had been issued prior to this. They're also appealing to all the companies to maintain their operation, otherwise, according to law, work obligation would have to be imposed. And at the same time, children are called upon to continue attending school. So they're persistently trying to maintain a so-called normal daily life and work in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 1 it says all citizens are called upon. Does that mean that there are any exceptions whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is about and to whom it refers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to all citizens who are not members of legitimate military forces to turn in weapons to the public security station by a determined dead-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are Serbs exempt from this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody is exempt. This is about all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3901, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us just devote some attention to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please have 65 ter 20382. But let's stick to a chronological order and instead have 65 ter 18922. It seems that we still haven't received a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document represents and can you please read the first and the penultimate bullet point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report about the engagement of the municipal civilian defence staff. In the first paragraph it says that after war operations in the area of town, the staff became involved in the evacuation of the population who did not take part in putting up resistance in other parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please read the penultimate one.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A convoy was set up in order to deliver goods for the population of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence? And can the next one be admitted under the same number because this document relates to the period up to October 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, all he's done so far is what Mr. Robinson criticised me for right at the beginning, which is read out two parts of it. I don't think there was a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question is always one and the same. Since we know that he studied Mr. Brown's findings and documents, how does this document fit with his findings as opposed to those of Mr. Brown, taking into account that the population who was not taking part in the resistance was moving from one part of the town to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, again, that was extremely leading. I know he was trying to explain, but -- I'm a little tired but reading the transcript all the witness has said is this first part says this and this other part says this. And I thought he was just reading it out. I can't tell if he was reading it verbatim because I can't read it, but that's what appeared to be happening. I have no problem with him asking some more questions about the document. I don't think it's admissible yet -- or marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About the first question and answer, what document is this about, this is report of something -- but I take it you have some further questions, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can this evacuation of the population not taking part in combat from one part of town to another be qualified as a criminal offence? And according to our Law on Defence, how is this kind of operation carried out by the civilian protection defined?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be qualified as a crime under the Law on Defence. It is an obligation to have a population be moved from a war-torn zone to an area where there are no such operation for security reasons. And this document demonstrates the efforts made by this organ, specifically the civilian protection and other organs to whom they are answerable for their work, to create conditions for ensuring protection for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if Mahala is in the town and whether there was any civilian population in Mahala and were there any paramilitary formations there, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mahala is a suburb, an area, that is part of the municipality, and at the time of these events it was a stronghold of armed Muslim forces that did not want to hand-over weapons and who opened fire in the attempt to -- by the Serbian forces to enter, in order to disarm them, or rather, to collect those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what happened to the population from Mahala in the fighting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness said: "... it was a stronghold of armed Muslim forces that did not want to hand-over weapons and who opened fire in the attempt by the Serbian forces to enter, in order to disarm them ... or to collect those weapons. Since the witness is not testifying as a fact witness, can Mr. Karadzic or the witness give me a cite to the document that says that in Mahala fire was opened on the Serb units when they came to try to collect weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
